analysis.investment_thesis: DCM Shriram's earnings yield of ~6.4% (EBIT 1,330 Cr / EV ~20,920 Cr) is marginally above the floor, but ROIC of ~12% (confirmed by company-reported ROCE of 11.4%) is well below the 20% threshold — the Magic Formula needs BOTH metrics to be strong, and ROIC here signals a mediocre, capital-intensive conglomerate. With net profit in structural decline (from 1,067 Cr in FY22 to 604 Cr in FY25) and massive capex cycles, there is no margin of safety.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 8.5% over 9 years and expanding operating income CAGR of 11.4% show moderate compounding capability
OCF positive in all 5 of 5 years, and 620 Cr of cash on balance sheet provides liquidity buffer
Diversified business (chemicals, sugar, Fenesta windows, agri) provides some cyclical hedge
key_risks: ROIC/ROCE of 11.4% is deeply below the 20% threshold — this is a capital-intensive business that earns mediocre returns
Net profit has nearly halved from peak 1,067 Cr (FY22) to 604 Cr (FY25) — a structural earnings decline, not a one-time blip
Massive capex cycle: 758 Cr (FY22) → 1,804 Cr (FY23) → 1,319 Cr (FY24) → 859 Cr (FY25), with CWIP hitting 2,615 Cr — this destroyed FCF for 2 consecutive years
red_flags: Forward P/E of 28.61x is HIGHER than trailing P/E of 27.40x — the market expects earnings to decline further, not recover; this makes the earnings yield even less attractive going forward
Free cash flow was negative in both FY23 (-493 Cr) and FY24 (-514 Cr) — the heavy capex cycle is consuming all operating cash generation
ROE of only 8.66% on a book value of 7,225 Cr means capital is being destructively deployed relative to cost of equity
analysis.detailed_analysis: EV = Market Cap 19,011 + Total Debt 2,529 - Cash 620 = 20,920 Cr. EBIT (Operating Income FY25) = 1,330 Cr → Earnings Yield = 6.36%, just barely above the 6% threshold. Capital Employed (equity 7,225 + debt 2,529 - cash 620) = 9,134 Cr → ROIC = 14.6%, but the company-reported ROCE of 11.4% is likely more accurate accounting for all capital. Neither metric clears my thresholds convincingly. Chemicals/PVC and sugar are commodity cyclicals — the FY22 profit peak of 1,067 Cr was a commodity supercycle windfall, not sustainable earnings power. The massive CWIP investment (peaked 2,615 Cr) suggests management is betting on a capacity expansion cycle just as profitability is declining — that's exactly the kind of value-destroying behavior I avoid.
